title: India's rice now sells for about $100 a tonne less than Thai rice
subtitle: Thai and Vietnamese rice prices are near two-year highs, Indian prices slipped, and officials say no new limits are planned on broken rice exports.
content_html:
Picture two rice sellers at the same market. One asks $490 for a big bag. The other asks about $390 for a bag that looks much the same. Buyers will walk to the cheaper stall. That is roughly where world rice stands this week, and India is the cheaper stall.

On 7 November 2026, a weekly price round-up by Reuters, carried by The Economic Times, showed rice from Vietnam and Thailand at close to two-year highs, while India's prices slipped. On the same day, two government officials told Mint that India does not plan any new limits on exports of broken rice. Put together, the two reports point one way: Indian rice is cheap, and the door for selling it abroad stays open.

What does "5% broken" even mean?

When rice is cleaned and polished in a mill, some grains snap into pieces. Traders sort rice by how many pieces are mixed in. "5% broken" means about 5 out of every 100 grains are bits, not whole grains. "100% broken" rice is made only of those small bits. It costs less than other grades, which is why it sells well in Africa, Milling MEA notes.

Parboiled rice is rice that is partly boiled while still in its husk, then dried and milled. This short video shows how it is made.

The price gap in plain numbers

According to the Reuters report, Vietnam's 5% broken rice was offered at $480 to $490 per tonne, up from $470 to $480 a week earlier. That is its highest level since December 2024. Thailand's 5% broken rice rose to $490 to $495 per tonne, its highest since January 2025.

India went the other way. Its 5% broken parboiled rice was quoted at $382 to $386 per tonne, down from $387 to $392 the week before and the lowest since 8 October. Indian 5% broken white rice was priced at $389 to $393 per tonne.

So a buyer in Africa or Asia can save roughly $100 on every tonne by picking Indian white rice over Thai rice. A tonne is 1,000 kg, the same as 40 bags of 25 kg each. On an order of 10,000 tonnes, a gap of $100 a tonne adds up to $1 million.

Why are Thai and Vietnamese prices climbing?

Traders quoted in the same report gave three reasons. First, the Philippines is buying rice from Vietnam again. Second, some rice areas in Thailand were flooded, so there is less grain to sell. Third, worries about El Nino, a weather pattern that can weaken rains, and a long wait until the next crop are keeping prices up.

Vietnam's sales are also strong. Its rice exports in October rose 37.2% from a year earlier to 475,000 tonnes, taking January to October shipments to 6.83 million tonnes, according to government figures quoted by Reuters.

Why is India's rice getting cheaper?

New rice is reaching the market. A Kolkata-based exporter told Reuters that new-season paddy arrivals (paddy is rice still in its husk, straight off the field) have started to pick up in northern states. That fresh supply is helping meet strong demand from buyers in West Africa.

The government's own stores are also full. As of 1 September, rice stocks in the central pool, the grain the government holds for ration shops and emergencies, stood at 39.05 million tonnes, with another 30.75 million tonnes of bought paddy waiting to be milled, Mint reported using Food Corporation of India data. Rice and wheat together came to 87.05 million tonnes.

The government also expects to buy 70.86 million tonnes of paddy in the 2026-27 kharif season (the crop sown with the monsoon), according to the food ministry estimate quoted by Mint. With that much grain on hand, officials see no need to stop exports.

The story of broken rice: banned, then freed

Broken rice has had a bumpy few years. India banned broken rice exports on 9 September 2022 over worries about supply at home, and lifted the ban on 7 March 2025, Mint notes.

When the ban was lifted, India's rice reserves, including unmilled paddy, stood at 67.6 million tonnes as of 1 February 2025, far above the government's target of 7.6 million tonnes, Milling MEA reported. In 2022, India sold 3.9 million tonnes of broken rice abroad, mainly to China for animal feed and to African nations like Senegal and Djibouti for people to eat.

Exporters hoped for a quick comeback. B.V. Krishna Rao, president of the rice exporters' body, said at the time: "we anticipate exporting around 2 million tons of this grade in 2025". The real number was lower. India shipped 8.08 lakh tonnes of broken rice in calendar year 2025, according to Mint. That is well under half of the 2 million tonne hope.

What the "no new limits" news means

"As of now there is no such proposal to impose any kind of restrictions on shipments for broken rice," one of the two officials told Mint. Both officials asked not to be named, and the food ministry had not answered Mint's questions when the report went out.

India produces around 5 to 6 million tonnes of broken rice a year. It is mostly used as feed for poultry and other animals, and to make ethanol, a fuel mixed into petrol, Mint reports citing the government.

India's choices move the whole world market. India's rollback of its rice export rules helped bring a 29% fall in global rice prices in 2025, which in turn helped cool food prices in countries like Senegal, Benin and Bangladesh, according to a World Trade Organization report cited by Mint.

This short video looks back at 2023, when India, a giant in world rice trade, closed the tap on many rice exports.

Who feels the change?

  • Indian exporters: Indian white rice sells for about $100 a tonne less than Thai rice this week, and new paddy is helping meet strong demand from West Africa, the Reuters report says.
  • Farmers: the government plans to buy 70.86 million tonnes of paddy this season, and 6.49 million tonnes had already been bought by 5 November in the 12 states the portal covered, Mint reports.
  • Buyers abroad: countries like Senegal, Benin and Bangladesh depend heavily on Indian rice, as per the WTO report Mint cites, so steady export rules matter for their food prices.
  • The worry: both reports point to El Nino. Traders say it is keeping prices up, and Mint says it raises concerns over the next crop.

For now, the picture is simple. Thai and Vietnamese rice is getting dearer, Indian rice is getting cheaper, and the government says the export door stays open.
